On a rainy afternoon, Jason was walking home from school when he heard a small sound under a bench. He bent down and saw a tiny grey kitten. It was wet and it was shaking.

Jason poured some milk into a saucer, but his mother stopped him. "Milk isn't good for kittens," she said. "Let's give it some water and ask the vet."
The next day, they took the kitten to the vet. The vet checked it and said it was healthy. She also found a small tag inside its collar with a phone number on it. Jason's mother called the number. Half an hour later, a girl and her father arrived. The girl cried with happiness when she saw her kitten.

Last Friday, our school held its winter concert. I was nervous because I had to play the piano in front of everyone. I practised every day for a month, but my hands were still shaking before the concert.
Before my turn, the choir sang three songs and the dancers performed a lion dance. The lion dance was so exciting that everyone clapped loudly.
Then it was my turn. I walked onto the stage and sat down at the piano. At first, I played too fast because I was nervous. However, I took a deep breath and slowed down. After that, the music sounded much better.
When I finished, the audience clapped and cheered. My parents were sitting in the third row, so I could see them smiling. My little sister waved at me.
After the concert, my music teacher said, "You were brave, and you didn't give up." I felt very proud. Next year, I want to play a duet with my best friend.

passage.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
passage.text:
Sleep is very important for children, but many children in Hong Kong don't get enough. Children aged nine or ten need about nine to eleven hours of sleep every night.
When we sleep, our bodies rest and grow. Our brains also sort out everything we learned during the day, so good sleep helps us to remember things. If we don't sleep enough, we feel tired and grumpy. We also find it hard to concentrate in class.
There are some easy ways to sleep better. First, try to go to bed at the same time every night, even at weekends. Second, stop using phones and tablets an hour before bed because the bright screens can keep your brain awake. Third, keep your bedroom dark and quiet.
Some people drink sweet drinks or eat big snacks before bed. However, this can make it harder to fall asleep. A glass of warm milk or water is a better choice.
So tonight, put down your phone, turn off the light and get a good night's sleep!

Joey and his friends wanted to play football on Saturday, but it rained all morning. They were disappointed because they had planned the game for weeks.
"We can't play outside, so what can we do?" asked Joey.
"We could go to the sports centre," said Raymond. "However, it's expensive, and we would need to book it first."
Joey's mother had an idea. "Why don't you make a football game at home? You can use paper, cardboard and bottle caps."
At first, the boys thought it was a silly idea. But they were bored, so they decided to try. Raymond drew the pitch on a big piece of cardboard, and Joey cut out the goals. Ken used bottle caps as players because they could slide easily on the cardboard.
By the afternoon, they had invented their own rules and played twenty games. Ken won the most games, although Joey scored the best goal.
When the rain stopped, the boys didn't want to go outside. "Let's play one more game!" said Raymond.

passage.text:
Every year, on the fifth day of the fifth month of the lunar calendar, people in Hong Kong celebrate the Tuen Ng Festival. One of the most exciting events is dragon boat racing.
A dragon boat is long and narrow. It has a dragon's head at the front and a tail at the back. There are usually twenty paddlers in each boat. They sit in pairs and paddle at the same time. A drummer sits at the front and beats a drum to help them keep the rhythm. A steerer stands at the back and controls the direction of the boat.
Teamwork is very important. If the paddlers don't move together, the boat goes slowly or even turns in circles. Teams practise for months before the races.
On festival day, thousands of people watch the races at places like Stanley and Tai Po. They cheer, eat rice dumplings and enjoy the summer sun. Many families make the trip every year because it is such a fun tradition.

passage.text:
Hong Kong has beautiful beaches, but many of them have a big problem: plastic rubbish. Every day, people throw away millions of plastic bottles, bags and straws. Some of this rubbish ends up in the sea.
Plastic is very dangerous for sea animals. Turtles sometimes eat plastic bags because they look like jellyfish, their favourite food. Fish and seabirds can get stuck in old fishing nets and plastic rings. Plastic also breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics. These pieces are so small that fish eat them by mistake.
The good news is that we can all help. We can bring our own bags when we go shopping. We can say no to plastic straws and use a refillable water bottle. Some schools also organise beach clean-ups. Last year, students from one school in Sai Kung collected more than two hundred kilograms of rubbish in one morning!
If everyone makes small changes, our sea will become cleaner and safer for the animals that live in it.

passage.title: Amazing Animal Abilities
passage.text:
Animals can do some amazing things. Some of them can do things that people can't do at all.
A cheetah can run faster than any other land animal. It can reach about 100 kilometres an hour, but it can only run this fast for a short time. After that, it needs a long rest.
An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through very small holes. It can also change the colour of its skin to hide from enemies.
Many birds can fly, but the hummingbird can do something special: it can fly backwards! It can also hover in one place while it drinks from a flower.
A long time ago, people thought that animals couldn't use tools. Now we know that some can. Chimpanzees can use sticks to catch insects, and some crows can bend wires into hooks to get food.
Next time you visit a zoo or watch a nature programme, think about what each animal can do.

passage.title: When Grandpa Was a Boy
passage.text:
Last weekend, I asked my grandpa what life was like when he was ten years old. His answers surprised me.
"When I was a boy, I couldn't watch TV every day," he said. "Only one family in our building had a television. On Saturday nights, all the children could go to their flat to watch cartoons."
Grandpa lived in a village in the New Territories. He couldn't take the MTR because there wasn't one. "We could walk to school in twenty minutes, but in the rainy season, the path was very muddy."
He could swim very well because he swam in the river near his village every summer. "Could you swim in the river now?" I asked. Grandpa laughed. "No, the river isn't there any more. There are tall buildings now."
Before I left, Grandpa said, "You can do so many things I couldn't do. But remember, we were happy too. We didn't need much to have fun."
I think about his words a lot.

In a small workshop, there lived a robot called Bolt. Bolt could tidy rooms quickly and carefully, but he was unhappy. Every night, his owner, an old inventor called Dr Lau, worked late and forgot to switch Bolt off.

That night, Dr Lau made a soft blue light for Bolt's charging corner. He also wrote a new rule on the wall: Everyone rests at ten o'clock, including inventors!
The next morning, Bolt tidied the workshop happily. He even sang a little song as he worked.

passage.title: Super Spiders
passage.text:
Many people are afraid of spiders, but these small animals are actually very useful. Most spiders are harmless to people, and they eat lots of insects such as flies and mosquitoes.
Spiders make silk inside their bodies. They use it to build webs, wrap their food and even travel. Young spiders can float through the air on a long thread of silk. This is called ballooning.
Spider silk is amazingly strong. For its weight, it is stronger than steel! It is also very stretchy, so it doesn't break easily when an insect flies into the web. Scientists are carefully studying spider silk because they want to make stronger ropes and better clothes.
Spiders are also patient hunters. Some spiders wait silently in their webs for hours. Others, like the jumping spider, hunt actively. A jumping spider can jump more than twenty times its own body length!
So next time you see a spider, don't scream. Look closely instead. You might see something truly impressive.

passage.text:
For Christmas, Ryan got a puzzle with one thousand pieces. The picture on the box showed a lighthouse by the sea at sunset.
On the first day, Ryan worked eagerly for three hours. He found all the edge pieces and finished the frame. On the second day, he started the sky. But the sky was all orange and pink, and every piece looked the same. Ryan tried and tried, but nothing fitted.
"This puzzle is impossible!" he shouted, and he pushed the pieces away angrily.
His older sister, Joanne, sat down next to him. "It isn't impossible," she said calmly. "You're just looking at it the wrong way. Sort the pieces by shape first, not by colour."
Ryan was unsure, but he tried it. He made piles of pieces with two knobs, three knobs and four knobs. Slowly, the sky began to fit together.
Two weeks later, Ryan placed the last piece. He took a photo of the finished puzzle and proudly sent it to his grandparents.

passage.title: Staying Safe in the Hot Sun
passage.text:
Summer in Hong Kong can be very hot. When the Observatory issues a Very Hot Weather Warning, you should be extra careful outdoors.
First, you must drink plenty of water, even if you don't feel thirsty. You should carry a water bottle with you all the time.
Second, you should wear light-coloured, loose clothes. Dark colours take in more heat. A hat and sunglasses will protect your head and eyes.
Third, you shouldn't stay in the sun for too long, especially between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m., when the sun is strongest. If you play sports, take breaks in the shade.
You must also put on sun cream before you go out. Put on more after swimming or sweating a lot.
If someone feels dizzy, has a headache or feels sick, they might have heatstroke. Let's remember what to do: move them to a cool place, give them water to sip slowly and tell an adult at once.
Would you like to stay healthy this summer? Then follow these simple rules!

passage.title: The Class Trip Vote
passage.text:
Mr Yeung's class had won the school tidy classroom competition. Their prize was a class trip, but they had to choose where to go.
"Let's go to the beach!" said Anson. "We could swim and build sandcastles."
"We shouldn't go to the beach in March," said Kayla. "The water will be too cold. Why don't we go to the Wetland Park? We could see the birds."
"Would you like to go to a farm?" asked Ivan. "We could pick strawberries. My cousin went last month and loved it."
Mr Yeung wrote the three ideas on the board. "You must listen to each other before you vote," he said. "Think about the weather, the cost and what everyone can do."
The class talked about each idea. Anson agreed that the water would be cold. Some students worried that the farm was very far away. In the end, they voted, and the Wetland Park won with eighteen votes.
Anson wasn't upset. "Can we go to the beach in June?" he asked with a grin.
